stem: Which of these is NOT part of a complete set of financial statements under IAS 1?

options.rationale: Correct: it is an internal working.

options.content: The statement of changes in equity
options.rationale: It is one of the required statements.
It is one of the required statements.
The notes are part of the set.

explanation: A complete set contains the statements of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, financial position, changes in equity and cash flows, and the notes.

stem: Under IAS 2, inventory is measured at:

options.content: the lower of cost and net realisable value
options.rationale: Correct: this applies prudence.

options.content: the higher of cost and net realisable value
options.rationale: That would anticipate profit.
Selling price includes profit not yet earned.
Replacement cost is not the IAS 2 measure.

explanation: IAS 2 requires inventory to be valued at the lower of cost and NRV, so losses are recognised immediately.

stem: Which cost formula for inventory is NOT permitted by IAS 2?

options.rationale: FIFO is permitted.
Weighted average cost (AVCO) is permitted.
Specific identification is allowed for non-interchangeable items.
Correct: it is not permitted.

explanation: IAS 2 allows FIFO, weighted average cost and specific identification for items that are not interchangeable, but not LIFO.

stem: An item of inventory cost US\$12.50 per unit. It can be sold for US\$14.00, but US\$3.50 of selling costs will be incurred per unit. At what value per unit should it be included in inventory?

options.rationale: Cost is higher than NRV, so it cannot be used.
Selling price is ignored in IAS 2 measurement.
Selling costs have been added instead of deducted.
Correct: NRV 14.00 - 3.50 = 10.50, which is lower than cost.

explanation: NRV = 14.00 - 3.50 = 10.50. This is below cost of 12.50, so inventory is valued at 10.50.

stem: A store holds three items. Item 1: 620 units, cost 5.80, selling price 7.40, selling costs 0.90 per unit. Item 2: 340 units, cost 14.20, selling price 15.50, selling costs 2.80. Item 3: 1,100 units, cost 2.15, selling price 3.40, selling costs 0.40. All amounts are in US dollars. What is the total value of inventory under IAS 2?

options.rationale: Total cost has been used: the write-down on item 2 was missed.
Correct: each item at the lower of cost and NRV (item 2 at NRV 12.70).
NRV was used for every item, including those where cost is lower.
Selling prices have been used.

explanation: Item 1: cost 5.80 (NRV 6.50); item 2: NRV 12.70 (cost 14.20); item 3: cost 2.15 (NRV 3.00). Total = 3,596 + 4,318 + 2,365 = 10,279 (computed by item).
hints: Compute cost and NRV per unit for each item and use the lower.

stem: What does the going concern assumption mean?

options.content: The business will make a profit in every future year
options.rationale: Going concern concerns survival, not profit.

options.content: The business will carry on trading in the foreseeable future
options.rationale: Correct: assets are not valued as if closure were planned.

options.content: The business has no loans or other debts outstanding
options.rationale: It does not mean the absence of debt.

options.content: The business is owned by one person or by one family
options.rationale: Going concern is unrelated to ownership.

explanation: Statements are prepared on the basis that the business will continue; otherwise assets would be valued at break-up values.
hints: What if the directors planned to close the business?

stem: Inventory with a cost of US\$9,400 and an NRV of US\$6,100 is included at cost in the closing inventory. What is the effect on profit and on inventory?

options.content: Profit and inventory are both understated by US\$3,300
options.rationale: Valuing above NRV overstates them.

options.content: Profit is overstated but inventory is correct
options.rationale: Inventory is also overstated.

options.content: Profit and inventory are both overstated by US\$3,300
options.rationale: Correct: the loss has not been recognised.

options.content: There is no effect because the goods are not yet sold
options.rationale: IAS 2 requires the loss to be recognised now.

explanation: Closing inventory is too high by 3,300, so cost of sales is too low and profit is overstated by the same amount.
hints: Closing inventory is deducted from cost of sales.

stem: A loan of US\$30,000 is repayable in ten months' time. In the statement of financial position it should be shown as:

options.rationale: It will be paid within twelve months.
Loans are not part of equity.
Correct: it is due within twelve months.
IAS 1 does not allow offsetting of this kind.

explanation: A liability due within twelve months of the reporting date is current, whatever the original term of the loan.
hints: Look at the time to repayment.

stem: If the net realisable value of an item of inventory is higher than its cost, the item is included at net realisable value.
explanation: False. Inventory is never valued above cost; the gain is recognised only when the goods are sold.

stem: IAS 1 generally does not allow assets and liabilities to be set off against each other in the statement of financial position.
explanation: True. Offsetting is allowed only when a standard permits it.

stem: Match each IAS 1 principle to its meaning.

right.content: The business will continue for the foreseeable future
Items are recognised when earned or incurred, not when cash moves
Presentation and classification stay the same from year to year
Omitting an item could change users' decisions

explanation: Each is a general principle of presentation under IAS 1.

stem: Complete the IAS 2 rule.

payload.template: Inventory is valued at the lower of {{blank:a}} and {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Cost is compared with net realisable value and the lower figure is used.

stem: Name the standard that deals with the presentation of financial statements.
explanation: IAS 1 sets out the form and content of financial statements.

stem: A company holds 2,400 units of an item at a cost of US\$3.90 each. The net realisable value is US\$3.10 per unit. Calculate the write-down required under IAS 2.
explanation: (3.90 - 3.10) × 2,400 = 1,920. Using the total cost gives 9,360.

stem: Gross profit before the IAS 2 adjustment was US\$61,250. A write-down of inventory of US\$4,200 is now required. Calculate the gross profit after the write-down.
explanation: The write-down increases cost of sales, so gross profit is 61,250 - 4,200 = 57,050.
workedSolution: 1. The write-down increases cost of sales, so gross profit is 61,250 - 4,200 = 57,050.

stem: A draft statement shows current assets of US\$92,300 and current liabilities of US\$61,400. A loan of US\$18,500 repayable in nine months was wrongly shown as non-current. Calculate the correct current ratio, as x : 1 to two decimal places.
explanation: Corrected current liabilities = 61,400 + 18,500 = 79,900; ratio = 92,300 ÷ 79,900 = 1.16 : 1. The draft ratio was 1.50 : 1.
workedSolution: 1. Corrected current liabilities = 61,400 + 18,500 = 79,900; ratio = 92,300 ÷ 79,900 = 1.16 : 1. The draft ratio was 1.50 : 1.
hints: The loan joins the current liabilities.

stem: Explain why inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

points.description: It applies prudence: a loss is recognised as soon as it is foreseen
It avoids overstating assets and profit by including inventory that will sell for less than its cost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prudence requires foreseeable losses to be recognised at once. Valuing inventory at the lower of cost and NRV prevents assets and profit from being overstated.

explanation: One mark for prudence and one for the effect on assets and profit.

stem: Explain why IAS 1 requires consistency of presentation.

points.description: Users can compare the results of one year with those of another
Changes in presentation could hide poor results or flatter the business
A change is allowed only if it gives more reliable information, and then the comparatives are restated

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Consistency lets users compare years. Without it, a change in presentation could hide poor results. A change is permitted only if it improves the information and the comparatives are restated.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Think about someone comparing this year with last year.

stem: State three items that are included in the cost of inventory and three that are excluded under IAS 2.

points.description: Included: purchase price, import duties and transport inwards (any three direct costs)
Excluded: storage costs (unless essential), administrative overheads, selling costs and abnormal waste (any three)
The rule: only costs of bringing the inventory to its present location and condition are included

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cost includes the purchase price, import duties and transport inwards. It excludes storage costs, administrative overheads and selling costs. Only costs of bringing the goods to their present condition and place are included.

explanation: One mark each for the included items, the excluded items and the principle.
hints: Which costs bring the goods to the place and condition for sale?

stem: The directors of a company wish to set off a loan receivable of US\$20,000 against a bank overdraft of US\$20,000 so that neither is shown in the statement of financial position. Evaluate their proposal.

points.description: IAS 1 does not allow offsetting unless a standard permits it, so both should be shown gross
Offsetting would hide the company's borrowing and the receivable, so users cannot judge liquidity or gearing correctly
Showing both gross may make the ratios look weaker, which may be the reason the directors want to set them off
Judgement: the proposal should be rejected because the statements must give a fair presentation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: IAS 1 does not permit the offsetting, so both items should be shown gross. Offsetting would hide the borrowing and mislead users about liquidity and gearing. The proposal should be rejected.

explanation: One mark each for the rule, the effect on users, the likely motive and a judgement.

stem:
Shurugwi Builders' Supplies Ltd counted the following at 31 December 2025. All amounts are in US dollars per unit.

| Item | Units | Cost | Selling price | Selling costs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Bricks | 2500 | 3.10 | 4.40 | 0.50 |
| Roof tiles | 1200 | 8.60 | 9.00 | 1.20 |
| Water pipes | 850 | 12.40 | 19.00 | 2.20 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the net realisable value per unit of roof tiles (to the nearest cent).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total value of the inventory under IAS 2.
parts.explanation: Bricks at cost 7,750; roof tiles at NRV 9,360; water pipes at cost 10,540; total 27,650.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Bricks at cost 7,750; roof tiles at NRV 9,360; water pipes at cost 10,540; total 27,650.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount by which inventory is written down.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the write-down affects the statement of profit or loss and the statement of financial position.

points.description: It increases cost of sales (or reduces closing inventory), so gross profit and profit fall by the amount of the write-down
Inventory in current assets is shown at the lower value
Retained earnings, and so equity, are reduced by the same amount

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The write-down reduces closing inventory and so increases cost of sales, lowering profit. Inventory in the statement of financial position is lower, and equity is reduced by the same amount.

parts.explanation: One mark for each statement affected.

explanation: This item tests the item-by-item valuation of inventory under IAS 2.
hints: Compare cost and NRV for each item separately.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the write-down of inventory required by IAS 2.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the corrected current ratio, as x : 1 to two decimal places.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Evaluate the effect of the corrections on the profit (draft US\$61,500) and on the liquidity of the company.

points.description: Profit falls by the write-down of 4,700 to 56,800
The current ratio falls from 1.91 : 1 to 1.19 : 1, a much weaker position, because the loan is now current
The company can still cover its current liabilities, but with a smaller margin, so lenders and suppliers will see more risk

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit falls by 4,700 to 56,800. The current ratio falls from 1.91 : 1 to 1.19 : 1, so the company is less liquid than the draft suggested, though it can still cover its current liabilities.

parts.explanation: One mark for the profit effect, one for the ratio comparison and one for the judgement.

explanation: This item applies IAS 1 and IAS 2 to a draft statement.
hints: A loan due within twelve months is current.
